title: Microtrace annotated batch replay and hypothesis log
content:
Quick summary
- Goal: reproduce a production tail-latency regression by replaying annotated microtraces so we can pin down scheduler vs kernel vs networking contributions.
- Approach: select 6 production incidents (p95->p99 gap), extract microtraces (per-request micro-events: enqueue, batch-formed, kernel-launch, first-byte), annotate with kernel-level perf counters and NVTX markers, then replay at scale against the local dev scheduler with controlled knobs.
- Current status: reproducible batch-latency spike for 3/6 traces using the replay harness; initial profiling points to increased kernel launch variance + a pre-kernel CPU stall on certain coalesced batches.

Why microtrace replay vs synthetic traces
- Synthetic workloads miss burst-alignment and real KV-cache hit patterns.
- Microtraces preserve per-request token budgets, prefix reuse, and arrival jitter which turned out critical for the regression.
- We add NVTX/trace annotations to correlate scheduler decisions with GPU kernel scheduling.

Data selection and extraction
- Incidents used: SR-2025-11-02-A, SR-2025-11-19-B, SR-2025-12-03-C, SR-2026-01-07-D, SR-2026-01-18-E, SR-2026-02-11-F (picked for clear p99 spikes and available microtraces).
- Extraction pipeline: trace-collector -> microtrace-extractor v0.9 -> annotate-with-kvcache.py -> produce replay bundle (.mtr.zip)
- Filtering: keep requests where model = fp16-ggml-7B-compatible, seq_len > 64, prefix_reuse >= 0.2.

Replay infra and knobs
- Harness: local replay node (replayctl) that can emulate arrival timestamps and token emission; hooks into the same scheduler binary as dev cluster.
- Key controlled variables:
  - batch_max_size (int)
  - timeout_ms (float)
  - fairness_weights (per-tenant urn, float)
  - kv_cache_prefill (bool)
  - kernel_quant_mode (none/4bit/8bit)
  - gpu_preemption_enable (bool)
- Commands used (examples):
  - replayctl --bundle sr-2026-01-07-D.mtr.zip --scale 1.0 --inject-jitter 0.0 --set batch_max_size=32 --set timeout_ms=6.0 --log microtrace.out
  - nvprof/nvtx command wrappers used to collect kernel timings during replay.

Microtrace annotation format (short)
- Each event is one line: <ts_ms> <req_id> <event> <meta>
- Events: enqueue, batch_form, batch_flush, kernel_launch, first_byte, end, kv_hit/miss
- Additional NVTX markers: SCHED_DECIDE, BATCH_QUEUE_OPEN, KERNEL_RUN_START, KERNEL_RUN_END

Observations from first-pass replays
- Reproducibility: 3/6 traces reproducible p99 spikes when batch_max_size <= 16 and timeout <= 6ms.
- Spike shape: affected requests show long gap between batch_flush and kernel_launch (~2-8ms variance) and often co-occur with increased batch formation churn.
- Kernel profile: when spike occurs, GPU kernel run times themselves don't increase significantly; the variance is almost entirely pre-kernel on the CPU path (scheduling, lock contention).
- Notable pattern: requests with high prefix_reuse (>0.6) and medium token-length (80-160) more likely to be victim requests in spike.

Profiling evidence
- Flame snapshots (CPU): heavy contention in threadpool_worker::pop_batch() -> schedule_lock, and occasional syscall blocks waiting on epoll when the queue drains rapidly.
- perf counters: high context-switch rates on core hosting scheduler thread during spike windows.
- nvprof timelines: kernel queues show uneven submission spacing; when submission is delayed the kernel queue backs up and subsequent flushes see longer submit latency.

Hypotheses (ranked)
1) Scheduler thread preemption and priority inversion: scheduler thread sometimes runs on a core with high syscalls causing it to miss wakeups and delay batch submission. This aligns with perf context-switch spike.
2) Batch coalescer thrashing: small timeout + aggressive prefill causes abort-and-reform cycles for batches, increasing scheduler CPU load and creating jitter.
3) Lock contention on shared batch-queue metadata when simultaneous microbursts from multiple tenants hit.
4) Kernel launch jitter due to driver-level serialization when too many small kernels are launched in tight succession (less likely given kernel times).

Mini-experiments run
- EXP-001: Force scheduler thread affinity to an isolated core -> p99 improved by ~18% on reproducible traces. (Good signal for hypothesis 1)
- EXP-002: Increase timeout_ms from 6 -> 12 for affected tenant -> p99 reduced but median increased slightly. Suggests tradeoff between fairness and median latency.
- EXP-003: Turn off kv_cache_prefill during replay -> little effect; not primary cause.
- EXP-004: Replace spin-lock on batch queue with MCS lock variant in dev branch -> reduced lock wait times in flame but only marginal p99 improvement (combined with core isolation had additive effect).

Metrics and numbers (sample from SR-2026-01-07-D replay)
- baseline (batch_max_size=16, timeout=6ms): p50=7.4ms, p95=18.2ms, p99=83.9ms
- scheduler-affinity (affine to core 11): p50=7.3ms, p95=16.9ms, p99=68.7ms
- timeout=12ms: p50=9.1ms, p95=15.5ms, p99=61.0ms
- combined (affinity + timeout=12ms): p99=48.3ms

Interpretation and recommended immediate mitigations
- Short-term: provide a tenant-facing knob to increase timeout_ms for high-latency-sensitive routes OR set scheduler affinity in Dedicated offerings as a safety net for critical customers.
- Medium-term: adopt scheduler-worker isolation (affinity + cgroup cpus) and revisit blocking syscalls inside scheduler code path (move epoll/poll out to helper thread).
- Longer-term: consider adaptive timeout that anneals based on short-term contention signals (context-switch rate, queue churn).

Open questions and next experiments
- Is the context-switch spike customer-pattern dependent (specific tenant codepaths) or a platform-level burst phenomenon? Need tenant-correlated traces.
- Does driver/kernel scheduling policy (CUDA stream priorities) interact with short-lived kernels differently across GPU models in us-west vs eu-west? Plan: run replay on g4dn vs a100 dev nodes.
- Can we observe same behavior under Dedicated (reserved capacity) hardware? (Might be masked by less noisy cores).

Action items (owners + ETA)
- Asha: spin up focused replay on A100 dev instance with EXP-001/002 config matrix + nvtx capture (ETA 2026-03-05)
- Diego: prototype moving epoll out of scheduler hot path and bench against microtrace replay (ETA 2026-03-12)
- Priya: collect tenant attribution for the 6 incidents and surface any custom tokenization/prefix patterns (ETA 2026-03-08)
- Ethan: PR for MCS lock experiment cleanup for bench (ETA 2026-03-10)

Notes to self / loose thoughts
- Keep a reproducible corpus of 50 short microtraces as a smoke test in CI for scheduler regressions. We currently only have large nightly replays which are slow.
- Consider adding an observability metric: 'scheduler-wakeup-latency' derived from NVTX delta between SCHED_DECIDE and BATCH_QUEUE_OPEN. Could be surfaced to console.
- If we expose a timeout knob to customers, default should be conservative (e.g., 10ms) and we should provide recommended presets (low-latency, cost-optimized).

Links and raw commands appendix (for replicating)
- extractor: python tools/microtrace/extract.py --incidents SR-2026-01-07-D --out bundles/sr-2026-01-07-D.mtr.zip
- replay: replayctl --bundle bundles/sr-2026-01-07-D.mtr.zip --scale 1.0 --inject-jitter 0.0 --set batch_max_size=16 --set timeout_ms=6.0 --trace nvtx,perf --out logs/sr-2026-01-07-D-replay.log
- nvprof capture example (wrapped): nvprof --profile-from-start off --export-profile nvprof.srq -- ./replay_binary --bundle ...

End of log.
- Recording: keep this doc as canonical experiment log for microtrace-based scheduler investigations.
- Followups: update after Diego's epoll refactor bench.
